Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

FINN 0.2.0

Changes that alter results

These change the numbers a fit or a simulation produces. Everything else in this release is new behaviour behind a new argument, a rename that keeps the old name, or documentation. Each row names the setting that restores the 0.1.0 result.

change new default restore 0.1.0
Offset of the trees likelihood at a simulated zero count fit(trees_offset = 0.01) trees_offset = NULL
Count gradients taken through the expected deaths and recruits, not through the draw fit(rb_gradient = TRUE) rb_gradient = FALSE
Exact binomial death draw instead of the moment-matched Gamma createProcess(mortality_draw = "binomial") mortality_draw = "gamma"
Exact recruit draw below lambda = 2 instead of the Gaussian approximation createProcess(regeneration_sampler = "refined") regeneration_sampler = "gaussian"
Limits of the mortality probability, per simulation step createProcess(mortality_floor = 0.001, mortality_ceiling = 0.999) 0.01 / 0.99
Recruitment capped by a Beverton-Holt term, with a prior on the cap finn()’s default regeneration process is regeneration_capped(cap = "all", prior = "max_obs_recruits", prior_lambda = 0.1) FINN::regeneration
Lower bound on the recruit dispersion, in the draw and the likelihood alike createProcess(theta_floor = 0.5) theta_floor = 0 or NULL
Growth enters mortality() in %/yr instead of as the raw rate createProcess(growth_scale = 0.01) growth_scale = 1
Binned competition takes its height quantiles over the live cohorts only createProcess(light_mask = TRUE) light_mask = FALSE
Additive recruitment floor createProcess(reg_floor = 1e-3) reg_floor = 0.2
A numeric loss_weights vector multiplies the baseline-scaled objective instead of replacing it fit(weight_scale = "auto") weight_scale = FALSE
predict() and simulateForest() leave requires_grad as they found it instead of switching every parameter on (#55) always -
resolveSiteIDs() numbers sites, patches and species by radix order instead of the collation locale’s always reproduces 0.1.0 where LC_COLLATE was already C
A hybrid growth process reads the growth predictors and a hybrid mortality process the mortality predictors (#72, B2) always - (0.1.0 and 0.2.0-rc fed each the other’s; identical where the two formulas are the same)

The sections The stem-count gradient, The death draw, The recruit draw, The mortality limits and The recruitment cap under The release in detail carry the measurements behind the first six rows.

The interface of finn() and fit()

Agreed for the release so that the two central functions read for an ecologist who does not know modelling terms. Every renamed or moved argument is still accepted under its old name, with a warning that names the new form, and gives the same result.

  • finn() writes its default processes in the signature instead of NULL: createProcess(func = mortality), createProcess(func = growth), createProcess(func = regeneration_capped) and createProcess(func = competition). They are exactly what NULL used to build, and NULL is still accepted. ?finn carries the model overview figure, says which equation each default is, that competition cannot depend on the environment, and has a complete build-estimate-simulate example.

  • finn(growth_rate = c("annual", "period")) replaces finn(growth_period_scale = ): it says what the growth column of the data is – the mean annual relative growth rate (default; TRUE was "period", the relative increment over the whole interval).

  • The recruitment floor moves to the regeneration process: createProcess(reg_floor = 1e-3). finn(reg_floor = ) is accepted with a warning and overrides the process’ value.

  • finn(recruit_obs_weight = ) is the last argument; it matters only for sampling designs that do not count recruits per hectare, and its explanation lives in ?recruitment.

  • fit() is titled Estimate the parameters of a FINN model and says that all processes are calibrated jointly. Its loss arguments stand together, each with one line and a link to the new help page ?finn_loss (likelihoods, aggregation, resolution, weights, the per-tree routes, loss_recruit); the input tables have the new help page ?finn_data (mandatory columns, missing values, incomplete series, what FINN fills in, env, disturbance, init_cohort, tree_data, the helpers).

  • fit(loss_weights = ) replaces fit(weights = ), so the name says these are the weights of the loss terms. fit(weight_scale = ) also takes TRUE (= "auto", the default) and FALSE (= "raw").

  • fit(loss_recruit = ) replaces fit(recruits = ); predict() and simulateForest() keep recruits =, where it is not a loss setting.

  • fit(control = finnControl()) collects the optimizer settings: optimizer, lr_scheduler, lr_scheduler_params, clip_norm and extra optimizer arguments such as weight_decay. lr, epochs and batchsize stay arguments of fit(). The four are still accepted as arguments of fit() with a warning.

  • fit(loss = ) is deprecated in favour of loss_family; it is kept as the last formal argument so that it does not partially match the loss_* arguments. loss_family also takes a partial named vector (c(trees = "nbinom") keeps the other five defaults).

  • fit() checks its input before anything runs and says what is wrong: a missing key or response column of data (a response with loss_family = "none" may be absent), species codes outside 1..N_species, duplicated rows, a plain data.frame is accepted; env without a predictor column (#64), with a missing value, with sites that do not share the same years, or without a year that data observes; disturbance without intensity, with values outside [0, 1], or over other sites and years than env. fit() and predict() warn when patches is given with init_cohort and differs (it is ignored, #66), and when patch_size differs from the one the model was last fitted or simulated with; predict()/simulateForest() default patch_size to the fitted one. fit(start_time = ) warns that it has no effect in 0.2.0.

  • The progress plot of fit(plot_progress = TRUE) shows every loss term over the whole range: it is redrawn each epoch with the y-axis fitted to the data, so a term that rises above its starting value is no longer cut off, and a term that is switched off is left out.

  • predict()/simulateForest() share one help page with a description; their examples fit two epochs first, so they run on the bundled data (an unfitted model has no environment scaling yet).

  • Removed from the exported interface, as nothing in the package, the tests or the vignettes used them: aggregate_results_old(), np_runif(), sample_poisson_relaxed(), the undocumented plot() method of a model (use ALE() and summary()), and the internal helpers groupby_mean() and index_species() are no longer exported.

Documentation and data preparation

  • The process functions growth(), mortality(), regeneration(), competition() and regeneration_capped(), summary() of a model, plot() of an ALE() object, compute_env_scaling() and dbh2ba() have runnable examples in the context of the fitting workflow; the print() method of finnControl() is documented with it. ?fit says in a few lines what makes a fit faster instead of reporting the benchmark behind it, the env_autoscale item is short and points to ?finn_data, and the help pages no longer cite issue numbers.

  • Examples for the fitting workflow (finn(), fit(), predict(), simulateForest(), predictTrees(), regeneration_capped(), regeneration_adult(), gated on an installed torch backend) and for the data helpers (makeObsData(), resolveSiteIDs(), makeInitCohorts(), climateDF2array()); the fitting vignettes gain sections on loss balancing, convergence checks, persistence and blocked holdouts, staged calibration, the recruitment cap and per-tree mortality scoring.

  • New datasets fia_tree_dt and fia_tree_test: the individual trees behind the mortality counts of fia_obs_dt and fia_obs_test (dbh, growth, fate and interval length per tree, all macroplot trees). The FIA vignette uses them to score mortality per tree (loss_aggregation = c(mortality = "tree")) and compares the size-mortality curve of that fit with the site-level fit.

  • resolveSiteIDs() returns env_dt with one row per site and year; it used to repeat each row once per patch, which climateDF2array() now rejects, so fit() failed on the output of the documented data-preparation pipeline.

  • fit() stops when the per-site path (loss_aggregation = "tree" or model$period_mode = "per_site") meets a data without a finite period_length. Every site’s window was then empty and all six loss terms were zero, so the fit ran to the end without scoring anything (#46). The data documentation no longer claims that period_length must be the same for every site.

  • fit() gains threads, torch’s intra-op thread count during the fit. The default NULL leaves torch’s setting alone, so OMP_NUM_THREADS or torch_set_num_threads() keep working. FINN’s forward pass is a chain of small tensor operations, and extra threads rarely pay (#48):

    • on macOS one thread was up to 30 % faster at the size of a BWI calibration batch (512 sites x 25 patches);
    • on a 64-core Linux node the thread count changed little, and only a single 2000-site batch gained from 4 threads.

    threads = 1 is the considerate choice when several fits share a machine. Where torch uses OpenMP the previous count is restored afterwards. torch’s native backend (macOS) allows one change per session, so there the session keeps the count, and fit() says so when an earlier setting prevents the change.

The release in detail

This release adds the model features developed for the FIA (US Forest Inventory and Analysis) and BWI (German Bundeswaldinventur) calibration projects. Every new argument defaults to the previous behaviour, with three exceptions that do not reproduce 0.1.0 and are marked in the table below: mortality(growth_scale = 0.01), createProcess(light_mask = TRUE) and createProcess(reg_floor = 1e-3). Two further exceptions repair the stem-count gradient and are on by default: fit(trees_offset = 0.01) and fit(rb_gradient = TRUE), both described under The stem-count gradient below. One further change reproduces 0.1.0 only on a machine whose LC_COLLATE was already C: resolveSiteIDs() now numbers sites, patches and species by radix order instead of the collation locale’s.

The two tables are the overview; the sections below them carry the detail.

The stem-count gradient

Two defects in how the trees term reached the parameters, both repaired here and both on by default (FINNverse/FINN#53).

The count likelihood added a constant to the predicted stem count so that log_prob stays finite where a species’ simulated count is exactly zero and the observed one is not. That constant was 1e-5 for "poisson" and 0.001 for "nbinom", which leaves the value finite and the gradient at y/offset – four orders of magnitude above every other term in the objective. Where the gradients are clipped per group, one such cell then rescales the whole mechanistic block. fit(trees_offset = ) exposes the constant and defaults to 0.01, on the scale of the predicted count. NULL restores the two historical values.

The simulator draws deaths and recruits and rounds them, and the gradient ran through both the reparameterised draw and the rounding’s straight-through surrogate, so the sampler’s noise reached the parameters. On the German inventory 97 % of the mortality gradient was draw noise (signal-to-noise 0.52 against 43 without it), which made a fit diverge or not depending on the host’s float kernels. fit(rb_gradient = TRUE) keeps the drawn, rounded count in the forward pass – a simulation is unchanged – and takes the derivative through n_at_risk * m and the expected recruitment instead. Against a 200-draw reference gradient the repaired direction agrees to a cosine of 1.000 in every parameter block at update_step = 1, where the unrepaired objective’s cosine is negative. FALSE restores the previous path.

Only fits that score trees are affected; a model scoring growth and mortality alone has no such term.

The death draw

mortality_draw gains "binomial", which is the new default, and "bernoulli".

"binomial" is the exact binomial, and it resolves by whether the draw has to carry a gradient. With rb_gradient = TRUE (also the new default) the drawn count is detached and the derivative comes from the expectation, so the draw is torch’s own binomial: exact in both moments at constant memory, and non-differentiable, which no longer matters. With rb_gradient = FALSE the gradient reaches the mortality parameters through the state – deaths enter trees, trees enters ba – so the draw must be differentiable, and it resolves to the moment-matched Gamma instead. Measured on that state path, the Gamma gives -39.36 against the expectation’s -39.32, while a straight-through Bernoulli gives -22.59 and the capped Poisson gives exactly 0.

Consequence worth knowing: under "binomial", switching rb_gradient changes the sampler as well as the gradient, so the two no longer simulate the same stand. Hold mortality_draw fixed to compare them.

"poisson" (a Bernoulli for one-tree cohorts, otherwise a capped Poisson) stays available. It is integer-valued and exact in expectation for small n*p, but its variance is n*p rather than n*p*(1-p) – measured 12.044 against 8.400 at n = 40, p = 0.3 – and it has no pathwise gradient. Combining it with rb_gradient = FALSE leaves the mortality parameters with exactly zero gradient, so that combination is now refused rather than silently fitted.

"bernoulli" is binomial_from_bernoulli(), repaired in this release (FINNverse/FINN#62): it returned exactly zero for every input, through an inverted trial mask and a reparameterised draw that was passed to a second torch_bernoulli(). It is exact in both moments and keeps a gradient path, but expands each cell to the largest cohort in the batch, so its memory grows with the largest trees value in the data.

The recruit draw

createProcess(regeneration_sampler = "refined") becomes the default. It samples exactly below lambda = 2 and drops the +0.001 offset and the 1e-4 clamp, which together imposed a recruitment floor of 0.0011 per cell-year – at a 0.0168 ha patch, 0.066 recruits per hectare and year per species. regeneration_sampler = "gaussian" restores the previous draw.

The mortality limits

The simulation clamps the per-cohort mortality probability before the death draw. That interval was hard-coded to [0.01, 0.99]; it is now createProcess(mortality_floor =, mortality_ceiling =) and defaults to [0.001, 0.999].

The bound is per simulation step, not per year, and the old floor is why a simulated low-mortality stand – a mature unthinned stand, a slow-growing species, an equilibrium run – lost stems the observations did not: at a 1 % floor every cohort is at risk at 1 % per step however low the fitted rate says it should be. The per-tree mortality loss was never bounded by it, so a fit could be correct while the trajectory it simulated was not.

The floor cannot simply be dropped: binomial_from_gamma()’s shape n*p/(1-p) degenerates as p -> 0. Measured with that draw it stays finite with an unbiased mean gradient down to 1e-4, but single-draw gradients grow heavy-tailed as n*p shrinks – the largest per-tree gradient is about ten times the old default’s at 1e-3 and about a hundred times at 1e-4 – so 1e-3 is the lowest tested value and is the new default.

The recruitment cap

regeneration_capped() replaces regeneration_saturation() (kept as a deprecated alias for one release) and becomes the default regeneration process. FINN::regeneration, unbounded as before, stays available and is now the opt-in.

Two things change beyond the name. The cap parameter reg_logK is created by FINN, so nothing has to be declared through custom_parameters any more; createProcess(cap = ) sets its resolution, "all" for one cap shared by every species and "species" for one per species.

And the cap carries a prior, because nothing else in the objective constrains it: a cap fitted freely runs to whatever the calibration window supports, which on a national inventory is far above anything observed. The penalty is prior_lambda * (log K - log prior)^2 per cap, the same form as the L2 pull of a staged calibration. prior = "max_obs_recruits" (the default) resolves it at the start of the first fit() from the largest observed recruitment rate per timestep, max(reg / period_length) – reg is the sum over an observation’s interval while the cap bounds one timestep’s mean – which is also the cap’s starting value; a later fit() continues from the trained cap rather than resetting it; a number sets the prior directly, on the same per-timestep scale; prior_lambda = 0 switches it off. With cap = "species" the prior is hierarchical – each species’ log cap is pulled towards the differentiable mean of all of them, so it penalises how far the species spread apart and leaves the overall level to the data.

The penalty is added after the loss_weights = "auto" baseline scaling, so prior_lambda means the same thing on every dataset.

What was broken

Most of these were silent. The last column says whether a result changes for someone who was affected.

defect results change?
fit(epochs = 0) ran two epochs (1:0) yes — it trained when asked not to
createProcess(upper = , lower = ) were overwritten with NULL, so every fit ran on the process defaults yes — a fit asking for tighter bounds ran unconstrained
createProcess(NN = ) was dropped inside create_nn() yes — the supplied network was not used
createProcess(growth_scale = ) was unvalidated: a bare NA divides by 1 and silently restores the 0.1.0 objective, 0 saturates mortality yes, and with nothing to signal it; now an error
A torch_load()ed model’s optimizer was reused although it no longer owned the model’s tensors yes — a crash (optim_ignite_*) or no training at all (optim_adam)
Observed-tree, size-class and quantile tensors of an earlier fit() were still evaluated in forward() yes — a stale term entered the loss
fit() set-up looked site and year up by linear scan, O(rows x sites) no — arrays bit-identical; ~20 min of set-up per fit at 32,686 sites
Observed-tree tensors were sized by patches, not by the patches the trees occupy no — light is per patch; predictTrees(patches = ) is now ignored
Per-tree growth and mortality were evaluated at the interval’s last year only, against interval observations yes, for the per-tree routes (new in 0.2.0)
predictTrees() returned rows in its own order, and failed on a model that had never been run yes — misaligned predictions
A tracked cohort the simulation killed left the scored set mid-window, so the scored sample was a function of the parameters yes, for loss_resolution = "tree" (new in 0.2.0)
A retained dead cohort, and any empty padding slot, moved the height quantiles of the binned competition and so the light of the living yes — masking is now the default; light_mask = FALSE keeps the old behaviour

A per-tree term was scored under a weight taken from the per-tree null while the cell term ran yes, on data with a constant census period
With sites observed in different years, each response’s loss summed one mean per observation year, so a year with ten trees weighed as much as one with thousands yes, for period_mode = "per_site" — the loss is now one pooled mean per batch
period_mode = "constant" with a per-tree term was silently overridden, with a false reason yes — now an error naming both halves
Cohort ids were enumerated flat over the whole array, losing the tree each cohort came from no — the link was recoverable, just not without a positional formula
resolveSiteIDs() numbered sites, patches and species through LC_COLLATE, so the same tables gave different integer ids on a German and on a C machine yes, off a C locale — the species number indexes par_growth / par_mortality, so a parameter row belonged to another species
$tree_deaths counted an earlier window’s ghosts among this window’s kills, and recorded liveness before the death draw diagnostic only — frac_killed was identically 0 on a one-year window
$tree_pred was not reset by fit(), and $tree_deaths reported NaN for a census with no fate target diagnostic only
A U+039B and a U+00D7 in ?fit, a stray \cr, two dangling \link targets, a @param on the wrong function no — the LaTeX manual and two R CMD check WARNINGs

New features

  • regeneration_adult_effect(): conspecific adults as an effect, not a gate. regeneration_adult() multiplies the whole potential recruitment by A / (A + A_half), so a species without adults on a site recruits only at reg_floor and bare ground cannot be colonised. The new process uses f(A) = f0 + (1 - f0) A / (A + A_half) with f0 = plogis(reg_adult_logitf0), a new custom parameter (shared or per species) for the share of the potential recruitment without conspecific adults (seed rain from outside, advance regeneration). f0 -> 1 is regeneration_capped(), f0 -> 0 is regeneration_adult(), which is unchanged. See ?regeneration_adult_effect and ?recruitment.

  • Bundled Oregon FIA data as package datasets. The calibration sample that the D-Fit_to_FIA and E-Mortality vignettes fit on now ships as lazy-loaded datasets in FINN’s input format: fia_obs_dt, fia_env_dt, fia_init_trees (200 training sites), fia_obs_test, fia_env_test, fia_init_test (200 disjoint holdout sites) and fia_species_dt (the shared species coding). They are ready for fit() / makeInitCohorts() without any file reading; see ?fia_obs_dt. The fia_*.csv files previously under inst/extdata are gone (the xz-compressed datasets are ~120 KB versus ~2.2 MB of CSV); the example_*.csv raw inputs for the data-preparation vignette stay.

  • Scoring individual trees, two ways. fit() can score growth and mortality per observed tree instead of per site, species and census. Both options take the same tree table in tree_data (one row per tree and census: siteID, year, patchID, species, growth, died, …) and are chosen explicitly: loss_aggregation = c(growth = "tree", mortality = "tree") predicts each OBSERVED tree (its measured dbh, light from the observed stand; the responses can be chosen separately and the initial cohorts may be binned), while loss_resolution = "tree" predicts each SIMULATED cohort that started as an observed tree along the model’s own trajectory (needs a cohortID column and one initial cohort per tree; combines with reanchor and teacher_forcing). loss_resolution = "tree" no longer takes a list of per-timestep target arrays — fit() builds those from the table and refuses any row it cannot place on an initial cohort. See ?fit, section Scoring individual trees, for the comparison. The two cannot be combined on one response. predictTrees() evaluates the first option on a fitted model. loss_resolution = "tree" reports $tree_deaths per census and epoch: the share of inventory-alive trees the simulation killed inside the window (frac_killed), the mean year it killed them (mean_kill_year), and the share that entered the window already dead from an earlier one (frac_ghost). Liveness is recorded after the death draw as well as before it: on the entering count alone a cohort killed in the window’s LAST year is indistinguishable from a survivor, so both numbers were undercounts and frac_killed was identically 0 on a one-year window. On the three-site, 24-tree fixture of tests/testthat/test-tree-loss.R the correction moves frac_killed from 0 to 0.167 and 0.208 on two one-year windows, from 0.250 and 0.042 to 0.292 and 0.125 on two three-year windows, and from 0.458 to 0.625 on a single four-year window, with mean_kill_year rising 1.82 to 2.40 there. frac_ghost is unchanged.

  • Training regimes: reanchor and teacher_forcing. Multiple shooting (reanchor = TRUE with anchor_cohorts, optionally anchor_mode = "merge" below anchor_min_dbh) rebuilds the simulated stand from the observed tree list at every census; teacher_forcing = TRUE resets it every year. The development branch’s fit(shooting = "multiple"), which re-anchored to the tree table itself, was dropped before release in favour of these.

  • Two repairs to the stochastic draws (createProcess(mortality_draw = , regeneration_sampler = )). Both are on by default in 0.2.0: mortality_draw = "binomial" and regeneration_sampler = "refined". mortality_draw = "gamma" and regeneration_sampler = "gaussian" restore the draws of 0.1.0, which are bit-identical to it (tests/testthat/test-identity.R, config sample_reg). The integer-valued alternative mortality_draw = "poisson" replaces the Gamma matched to the binomial’s first two moments by a Bernoulli draw where the cohort holds one tree or fewer and a Poisson capped at the cohort size otherwise: the default draw is rounded straight-through by the forward pass and then delivers 0.68-0.72 of the calibrated deaths for one-tree cohorts at annual probabilities of 0.01-0.10, and its pathwise gradient runs through a quantity the simulation discards. regeneration_sampler = "refined" drops the +0.001 Gamma offset and the 1e-4 probability clamp (both guard the Gaussian branch against a negative draw and a NaN gradient through log(0); neither hazard applies to torch_poisson) and samples exactly below lambda = 2. The offset and the clamp are a recruitment floor of 0.0011 per cell-year, which at a patch of 0.0168 ha is 0.066 recruits ha^-1 yr^-1 per species – over a hundred-odd species, as large as a temperate inventory’s whole ingrowth. Both repairs move the simulated stand at equilibrium by a factor of several in basal area and stem number while barely moving the fitted loss: the holdout cannot separate them, the simulated stand can.

  • fit(nonfinite = ). When one of the six loss terms is not finite at a timestep, "drop_term" (the default) leaves only that term out, still backpropagates the other responses there and counts the occurrences in model$nonfinite_counts; "skip_step" discards the whole timestep, which is what earlier versions did.

  • Per-predictor environmental scaling (env_autoscale). Previously every environmental predictor was standardised the same way. env_autoscale now takes a per-predictor specification — "auto" (z-score, the default), "identity" (leave as supplied), "0to1" (min-max), or a user-supplied function(x) returning list(center=, scale=) — given either as a single value applied to all predictors or as a named vector/list per predictor. Every mode is affine, so ALE interpretation stays invertible. The fitted constants remain accessible via compute_env_scaling() / apply_env_scaling(). Dispatch is fully backward compatible: the previous TRUE / FALSE / NULL forms behave exactly as before.

  • Recruitment observation weight (finn(recruit_obs_weight = )). An observation operator, not a weight of the loss term: it multiplies predicted and observed recruitment per ha alike before the regeneration likelihood, so that the likelihood scores the counts a sampling design actually tallies. In 0.2.0 it is applied under loss_family["regeneration"] = "nbinom" only (#65).

  • Period-scale growth scoring (finn(growth_rate = "period")). Scores growth over a multi-year remeasurement interval rather than a single step, for inventories whose growth is only observed between remeasurements.

  • Custom process parameters (createProcess(custom_parameters = )). Lets a user-supplied process function declare and calibrate its own named parameters, beyond FINN’s built-in per-species and per-environment coefficients.

Behaviour changes

  • Calibration runs on annual simulation steps: data preparation, bundled data and vignettes. One simulation step per ten-year remeasurement interval distorts the dynamics: recruitment, competition and growth act once per decade, and the per-step mortality floor and ceiling become limits per decade. On FIA Oregon a model calibrated that way grew to a bare-ground equilibrium of 100-170 m2/ha that was still rising; calibrated on annual steps it levels off at 45-60 m2/ha. So everything the package ships now uses one step per year:

    • makeObsData(rates = c("annual", "interval")): growth and mort are yearly rates by default, (dbh / dbh_before)^(1 / p) - 1 per tree and 1 - (1 - n_died / n_at_risk)^(1 / p) per cohort over an interval of p years, and the table carries period_length (years since the previous inventory). n_at_risk, n_died, growth_n and reg stay quantities of the interval, as fit() uses them: it averages the simulated yearly growth and mortality over the period_length years before a census, scores mort with the binomial weighted by n_at_risk, and sums the simulated recruits. The returned tree list gains growth, the tree’s rate in the same unit (rel_growth stays the interval increment). rates = "interval" returns the rates over the whole interval, as before.
    • resolveSiteIDs(time_axis = c("annual", "census")): year is the number of years since the first inventory (0, 10, 20 rather than 0, 1, 2), the first inventory is the initial state (initial cohorts, no observation row), and env_dt comes back with one row per site and year 1..Tmax, so it needs one row per calendar year (a static climate is repeated). env_dt now holds only siteID, year and the predictors, which is what fit(env = ) accepts (it carried the character siteName, which fit() refuses). time_axis = "census" keeps the inventory index of 0.1.0, but builds the initial cohorts from the first inventory, as the annual axis does; 0.1.0 took the second inventory (year == 1) for them, so 0.1.0 results are not reproduced exactly on the census axis either.
    • The bundled FIA datasets (fia_obs_dt, fia_env_dt, fia_obs_test, fia_env_test) are rebuilt on the annual axis from the same plots and sample: observations at years 10 and 20 (21 and 22 for two sites whose third inventory came late) with period_length, yearly growth and mortality, and env over years 1..22. Growth is now also tree-weighted across patches as makeObsData() defines it; the old table carried the unweighted mean of the patch means. ba, dbh, trees, reg and the counts are unchanged; example_env_dt.csv has one row per calendar year.
    • The vignettes, examples and tests that use these data simulate the 20 years between the inventories. The vignettes score a fitted model the way fit() does: the stand at the census year, growth and mortality averaged over the period_length years before it, and the expected recruits per hectare (r_mean_ha) summed over them. Results computed on the bundled data or with makeObsData() / resolveSiteIDs() defaults change.

  • The simulated rates of an interval are compounded as the observed rates are. makeObsData(rates = "annual") derives a yearly growth rate as (dbh / dbh_before)^(1 / p) - 1 and a yearly mortality as 1 - (1 - d / n)^(1 / p) over an interval of p years, but fit() compared them with the arithmetic mean of the simulated yearly rates over the period_length window. With one disturbance year in a window the two differ a lot: a mortality of 0.5 in one year and 0.01 in nine is observed as 0.0754, and the mean is 0.059. fit() now compounds the window the same way, growth as exp(mean(log1p(g))) - 1 and mortality as 1 - exp(mean(log1p(-m))), with the same masks as before: a year outside a site’s window or without trees counts as growth 0 and survival 1, and the denominator is the full period_length, since the observed rate is derived from the counts over the whole interval. Mortality is clamped below 1 - 1e-4 before the log (sigmoid saturates to exactly 1 in float32 above a logit of 17.3), growth is not clamped (the package’s growth is non-negative). The per-tree route follows for growth (loss_aggregation = "tree", loss_resolution = "tree", predictTrees()); its mortality was already the compounded interval probability against the tree’s 0/1 fate. The constant increment of finn(growth_rate = "period") is unchanged, as is the census axis, where one step is one interval. Vignettes D and E score the fitted models with the same functional. Fits on data with period_length > 1 change; the identity snapshots of the test suite were regenerated.

  • Mortality starts at about 2 % per year. The environmental response of mortality() started at torch’s random weights, i.e. at sigmoid(0) = 0.5 per step at the average environment, so on yearly steps an unfitted stand lost most of its basal area within ten years and the first epochs of a fit began from a dying stand. Without createProcess(initEnv = ) the response now starts with an intercept of qlogis(0.02) and every other weight 0 (with hidden layers the output bias carries the intercept); the species terms for light, size and growth move the start by at most about one logit unit. A formula without an intercept (~ 0 + temp) keeps torch’s start. ?finn, ?createProcess and ?mortality say so. Fits and simulations that did not set initEnv for mortality start from another point and so change.

  • Bare ground is bare: init_cohort = NULL starts with no stems. simulateForest() / predict() and fit() without an init_cohort used to start every patch with one 1-cm stem of every species, although the help said “empty patches”. That planted species the regeneration process would not recruit, so a bare-ground (equilibrium) run did not test the regeneration process: on FIA conterminous US a species of moist eastern sites grew to 62-73 % of 112-168 m2/ha at dry western sites where it barely recruits; from an empty start the same model ends at 30-61 m2/ha. Now every tree of such a run comes from the regeneration process. Results of runs without an init_cohort change; runs with one are unaffected.

  • Trees can grow up to 130 m, not 101 m. The upper bound of the fitted height parameter (first column of the competition parameters) is log(2.3) instead of 0.7. height() approaches (exp(parHeight) - 1) * 100 m as the diameter grows, so 0.7 capped every species at 101 m, below the 122-130 m physical limit of tree height (Koch et al. 2004), and a species given exactly 0.7 (as in the introduction vignette) was clamped with a warning. Fits that train the competition parameters change slightly, because the bound sets the scale on which the parameter is optimised. createProcess(upper = c(0.7, 2.0)) on the competition process restores 0.1.0.

  • The recruitment floor is 1e-3, not 0.2. createProcess(reg_floor = ) replaces a hard-coded additive floor of 0.2 on the expected recruitment of every species in every cell-year. At 0.2 the floor alone delivered about 13 stems per hectare per year over a 65-species FIA pool, against roughly 0.7 observed – the floor was the recruitment. It exists to keep the negative-binomial likelihood away from a zero mean, which 1e-3 does. createProcess(reg_floor = 0.2) on the regeneration process restores 0.1.0.

  • The binned competition masks padding out of its height quantiles. createProcess(light_mask = ) now defaults to TRUE. The cohort dimension is padded to the widest site x patch of the batch and an empty slot has height ~0, so unmasked the bin edges are set by how many empty slots happen to sit beside a stand. Measured on ten live cohorts of 55 to 8 cm: beside a batch neighbour holding ten cohorts their light runs 1.00, 0.76, 0.58, 0.44, 0.34, 0.27, 0.22, 0.19, 0.17, 0.16; beside a neighbour holding a hundred it is 1.00 for all ten – competition disappears, with the stand itself unchanged. Batch composition is not part of the model, so the unmasked quantile made the fitted objective a function of batchsize. This is a defect rather than a modelling choice, which is why it changes a default instead of arriving as an option. createProcess(light_mask = FALSE) reproduces results published before 0.2.0. continuous = TRUE compares pairs and was never affected.

  • A numeric weights vector multiplies the scaled objective, it no longer replaces it. fit(weights = ) used to bypass the "auto" baseline scaling entirely, so the six numbers acted on losses whose raw magnitudes differ by three orders of magnitude. Measured on BCI with the weight vector of the published configuration, c(0.1, 10, 1, 1, 1, 1): the raw baseline MSEs stand at dbh : ba : growth = 1246 : 26 : 1, so growth held 0.26 % of the objective at the start and 4.5 % at convergence, and ba’s nominal factor of ten was a factor of ten on a scale already 26x growth’s. Weights now multiply the baseline-scaled losses, where a weight reads directly as that response’s share. fit(weight_scale = FALSE) restores the old behaviour exactly and is what reproduces an analysis fitted before 0.2.0. Every fit now prints each response’s share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline, in both modes – the silence was the actual defect.

  • Site, patch and species ids are radix-ordered, not locale-ordered. resolveSiteIDs() assigned them through as.factor() and sort(), both of which order by LC_COLLATE: c("Acer", "abies_x") is that order under C and the reverse under de_DE.UTF-8. The species number indexes the fitted parameter matrices, so the same input file gave par_growth[1, ] to one species on one machine and to another species on the next, with nothing in the output to show it. Ordering is now sort(..., method = "radix"), which ignores the locale. Results are unchanged for anyone who ran under C; everyone else gets a different, and now reproducible, numbering, so ids in artefacts built before this release do not necessarily line up with ids built after it.

  • Growth enters mortality() in %/yr. The default mortality process now uses growth / growth_scale with growth_scale = 0.01, so the growth coefficient parMort[, 3] acts per 1 %/yr of annual relative growth. On the raw rate the term spanned only a few tenths on the logit between slow and fast trees even at the coefficient bound of -10 (in the BWI calibration 13 of 15 species sat at that bound). This is the one default that does not reproduce 0.1.0: createProcess(func = FINN::mortality, growth_scale = 1) recovers the old behaviour. Saved models keep the process function they were fitted with.

  • Per-site path: one mean per batch, not one per observation year. With sites observed in different years (period_mode = "per_site"), each response’s loss was the MEAN over the units of each observation year, and the years’ means were SUMMED. A year with ten trees then weighed as much as one with thousands (in the BWI split-census set-up the pre-drought half of 10 % of the trees carried 75 % of the mortality objective, the drought half 3 %). The loss is now one mean over all units scored in the batch (each year’s mean weighted by its share of trees / n_at_risk / growth_n / cells), which is also what the loss_weights = "auto" baselines measure; the reported history is that pooled mean. A batch that scores one observation year is bit-identical to before; the constant-period path is unchanged.

Performance

  • fit() set-up no longer scales with sites x rows. climateDF2array() (behind every response and environment array fit() builds, ~140 calls per fit with 15 species) looked each row’s site and year up by a linear scan, so a call cost O(rows x sites): ~90 s at 32,686 BWI sites, ~20 min of set-up per fit. The lookup is now a hash map, O(rows); the arrays are bit-identical.

  • Observed-tree tensors have the trees’ own patches. For loss_aggregation = "tree" and predictTrees(), the tree tensors were sized by patches (e.g. 25) although the trees occupy fewer patches (all BWI trees have patchID 1), and competition, growth and mortality ran on the empty ones in every batch. They are now sized by the number of distinct patchIDs in tree_data. Light is computed per patch, so no prediction changes; predictTrees(patches = ) is now ignored.

  • Fewer torch calls per time step in forward(). On the tensors of one batch (~30k elements) a torch op costs ~25 us of fixed overhead and the time loop made ~2000 of them per step, so the op count, not the arithmetic, sets the speed. The per-species aggregation of the rates, the recruits and the stand (growth, mortality, dbh, basal area, trees, regeneration) now scatters all its samples in one call (aggregate_species(), internal) and writes the masked tree-weighted means with torch_where() instead of two masked index assignments; trees$sum() > 0 is read with $item(); whether the gradients are yearly (no period_length anywhere) is decided once per call instead of by a reduction over y at every step. The results are bit-identical (checked on two BWI stage-2 calls: parameters, loss history, baselines, param_history, predictTrees()).

  • The per-tree scoring evaluates the window in one pass. loss_aggregation = "tree" and predictTrees() applied growth and mortality to the observed trees once per year of the remeasurement window (10 calls of each process per batch on the BWI data); the years are now a dimension of the tensors and the processes run once (mechanistic processes; hybrid ones keep the year loop). Same formula, but the sums over the years and over the trees are taken in another order, so the result is equal only to floating point precision: on two BWI stage-2 calls the fitted parameters after 3 epochs differ by at most 2e-6 (absolute, float32), the loss history by 6e-8 and predictTrees() by 3e-6 (FINN-bwi fits/2026-11-06-finn-speed-review).

Bug fixes

  • fit() no longer creates or overwrites an object counter in the global environment. The batch counter was advanced with <<-, which also left the local counter at 1: with several batches per epoch (batchsize smaller than the number of sites) $history, the progress plot and the plateau scheduler saw the last batch’s loss instead of the mean over the epoch’s batches. With one batch per epoch, the default, nothing changes.

  • A hybrid growth process is given the growth design matrix and a hybrid mortality process the mortality one. The environment list is ordered mortality, growth, regeneration, and the two were read by position, so createHybrid() growth was fitted and simulated on the mortality formula and vice versa. Regeneration and predictTrees() always read theirs by name, so the two routes disagreed for the same model. Nothing changes where the growth and mortality formulas are the same, which is every example in the package; formulas of different width stopped with “mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied”.

  • createHybrid(hidden = ) accepts a single hidden layer. hidden = 16L used to build the layer stack with 2:length(hidden), which counts backwards from 2 to 1, and the first fit() stopped with “Expecting a single value: [extent=0]”. The default hidden = c(50L, 50L) is unaffected.

  • predictTrees() checks that tree_data and env hold the same sites, that every observed year is in env and that the species ids are those of the model. The tree tensors follow the sites of tree_data and the environment array those of env, and torch’s gather accepts the shorter index, so a tree could be scored against another site’s climate without any message.

  • predictTrees() on a model that has never been fitted or simulated asks for patch_size instead of ending the R session. BA_stand() divided by a NULL patch size, which segfaults torch_div().

  • conditionalEffects(), ALE() and summary() pair each stand state with its own site’s and year’s predictors when env is not sorted by siteID and year. The recorded states follow the simulation’s sorted order and the predictors were taken in order of appearance.

  • conditionalEffects() and ALE() recompute when env or init_cohort is passed explicitly. The cache key is a fingerprint (row and column count, column names, column sums), so two different inputs could share it and the first call’s result was returned for the second.

  • createProcess() and createHybrid() find a formula that is held in a variable of the calling function (f <- ~ temp; createProcess(f, growth) inside a function used to stop with “object ‘f’ not found”).

  • predictTrees() puts the model in evaluation mode and on the scoring device before it predicts, as simulateForest() does. Straight after fit() the model was still in training mode, so a process with dropout returned different predictions on every call.

  • makeInitCohorts(dbh_binsize = ) adds up trees with na.rm = TRUE. A record without a stem count (trees = NA, e.g. a dead tree) used to turn its whole bin into NA, which lost the living trees of that bin (349 of the 5350 stems of fia_init_trees with dbh_binsize = 5).

  • mortality(debug = TRUE) returns the list of its components (light, environment, predM) instead of stopping with “object ‘shade’ not found”.

  • predict() and simulateForest() left requires_grad = TRUE on every parameter of the model they had just simulated, so a model frozen for a staged calibration silently unfroze as soon as it was simulated (#55). Both now restore the state they found.

  • createHybrid(NN = ) was documented as replacing the network architecture but was never stored, so a custom module was accepted and then ignored (#59). A non-NULL NN now raises an error; shape the default network with hidden, dropout and transformer.

  • A stand that dies out before a census is now scored. When every cohort of a batch had died, the padding pass left no cohort slot and the census step was not scored at all (the scoring required at least one slot), so a die-off before a census went unpenalised. An empty stand now predicts zero basal area, zero trees and the recruits of the window against the observations; dbh, growth and mortality have no prediction without a tree and stay unscored at such a step. The zero predictions carry no gradient (nothing is left to move), but the loss is reported, so a fit that kills its stands shows it in $history instead of a flat zero.

  • A model that never went through fit() simulated with the 0.1.0 Gamma death draw instead of the mortality_draw = "binomial" default, because the flag that selects the exact binomial (rb_gradient) was set only inside fit(). finn() now sets it to fit()’s default, so simulateForest() on a freshly built model, and a model rebuilt from saved parameters, draw deaths as a fitted model does (#70).

  • fit(epochs = 0) ran two epochs (1:0); it now runs the set-up only (data tensors, loss_baseline / loss_weights) and trains nothing.

  • fit() resets the observed-tree, size-class and quantile tensors of an earlier call (or a torch_load()ed model) before building those of the current one; stale tensors were otherwise still evaluated in forward().

  • createProcess(NN = ...) is no longer silently dropped inside create_nn().

  • createProcess(growth_scale = ) is validated. The value is used as a bare divisor inside mortality(), so every wrong value was silent: a bare NA is logical and coerces to TRUE, so growth / NA divides by 1 and reproduces the 0.1.0 objective exactly, with no warning and no NaN; NA_integer_ divides by -2^31; growth_scale = 0 saturates mortality to 0 or 1 across the whole stand. Anything but a single positive finite number, or NULL, is now an error at createProcess() time. Saved models are unaffected.

  • loss_weights = "auto" no longer explodes on a response that is constant over the scored cells. The intercept-only baseline is then a few float ulps rather than zero, so 1/baseline passed the <= 0 guard and produced weights of order 1e17 on a package fixture. Such a response is now left unscaled, with a warning naming it.

  • fit() resets $nonfinite_counts, so the end-of-fit warning reports this fit’s dropped terms rather than the total since the model was built.

  • Arguments that gate on isTRUE() are validated as logicals: fit(reanchor = ), fit(teacher_forcing = ) and createProcess(light_mask = ) accepted 1 and then silently behaved as FALSE. createProcess(reg_floor = ) is validated the way growth_scale is. fit(loss_aggregation = ) rejects a response named twice instead of keeping the first entry, and fit(env_autoscale = ) rejects a named entry that matches no predictor instead of silently scaling that predictor with the default.

  • **mortality()‘s growth coefficient is initialised on the scale growth enters on.** parMort[, 3] was drawn from U(-0.2, 0.2) regardless of growth_scale, so at the 0.01 default the same draw acted a hundred times more strongly. Measured on the four-site FIA fixture: an anchored stand of 1667 stems/ha at 25 cm drops to 1.0-7.5 stems/ha in a single year (mortality 0.93 to 1.00), against 28-75 stems/ha at growth_scale = 1. The range now scales with growth_scale; a custom mortality kernel without that formal keeps the old range. Random initialisations therefore differ from earlier versions’.

  • The identity fixtures gained a configuration with unequal scored units per observation year (per_site_unbal). Every existing per-site configuration carried the same number of cells in every year – 6 against 6 – and with equal counts the per-unit pooling of the per-site loss and the former sum of per-year means agree exactly, so no snapshot could see a change to that weighting. The new configuration is one species-census short in the first scored year, 5 against 6.

  • fit(folder = , checkpoints = ) writes each checkpoint to a temporary name and renames it. A kill or a full disk during the save used to leave a truncated .pt that torch_load() could not read.

  • fit() warns when the regeneration process is being calibrated while loss_family["regeneration"] is "none". No other response can train it: recruits reach dbh through a sigmoid of scale 1e-3, whose derivative is zero almost everywhere, and trees through a rounding whose forward value is 0 below 0.5 recruits per patch and species.

  • resolveSiteIDs() orders site, patch and species names with sort(..., method = "radix") instead of the collation locale; see Behaviour changes. Covered by tests/testthat/test-locale-stable-ids.R, which runs the function under C and de_DE.UTF-8 on names the two locales order differently.

  • fit() resets $tree_pred along with $tree_obs and $tree_deaths. It is written only by the per-tree branch of forward(), so a plain fit after a per-tree one left the earlier call’s predictions in place.

  • $tree_deaths skips a census that carries no fate target at all (died is NA for every row of it) instead of reporting NaN for frac_killed, window and frac_ghost, which are 0/0 there.

  • pred2DF() selects its index columns with with = FALSE instead of the ..dim_names prefix, which R CMD check reported as an undefined global.

  • fit() and predict() check that data, env and init_cohort hold the same sites and stop with the offending ids and the table they are missing from (#33). Before, a mismatch ended in a torch index error that named nothing, or silently paired a site with another site’s environment. The ids need not be 1:N: every array is indexed by a site’s position among the sorted ids. siteID must be integer-valued in data and env (the error points to resolveSiteIDs()). Covered by tests/testthat/test-site-sets.R.

  • Site ids that are not 1:N keep their identity end to end (#34). obsDF2arrays() numbers sites in radix order (independent of the locale, as resolveSiteIDs()), says so in a message instead of the former warning when the ids are not 1:N, and records the user ids as attribute "site_ids", which CohortMat keeps as $site_ids; a fitted model keeps the lookup from array position to siteID as $site_lookup; and predict() / simulateForest() return the caller’s own siteIDs instead of positions. For ids that are 1:N nothing changes. Patch and cohort ids are renumbered in radix order as well. Covered by tests/testthat/test-site-sets.R.

  • climateDF2array() stops on any (siteID, year[, month, day]) combination that appears more than once, identical or not, naming it (#35); the last row used to win silently. A missing combination is still NA. Covered by tests/testthat/test-climateDF2array.R.

  • The bundled fia_env_dt and fia_env_test hold one row per site x year (600 rows each). They repeated every row four times, once per patch of the source plot, all identical, so every environment array built from them is unchanged (dev/make_extdata.R now deduplicates; the two .rda files were deduplicated in place). The env_autoscale constants do move: the standard deviation (n - 1 denominator) over 600 instead of 2400 rows is 0.063 % larger, and a seeded fit on the z-scaled climate amplifies that, so the re-knitted vignettes D and E report slightly different fits.

  • feature_importance() permutes over distinct env rows. On an env with repeated site-year rows the copies received different permuted values, of which the environment array kept one at random, so importance values computed on such data change.

  • createProcess(custom_parameters = ) checks names against a fixed list of fields FINN sets itself (#42). A name that a later process sets, such as light_mask, used to pass, became a trainable nobody read, and turned the later assignment into a silent no-op. Covered by tests/testthat/test-processes.R.

Documentation

  • New help topic ?recruitment: the recruitment processes, the recruit draw, the dispersion theta and its floor, the regeneration likelihood and recruit_obs_weight, feeding observed recruitment, and a guide to which options to combine; the recruitment arguments of createProcess(), createHybrid(), finn(), fit() and simulateForest() point to it.

FINN 0.1.0

CRAN release: 2026-08-09

First public release.

FINN is a differentiable forest gap model: a cohort-based dynamic vegetation model whose demographic processes (competition, growth, mortality, regeneration) can each be a mechanistic function, a neural network, or a mixture of the two, all calibrated end-to-end by gradient descent.

Highlights of the current interface:

  • finn() assembles a model from one process per demographic component, each built with createProcess() (mechanistic) or createHybrid() (neural network).
  • simulateForest() runs a model forward; fit() calibrates one to data and predict() scores it, returning patch- and site-level results.
  • Per-response likelihoods: Gaussian ("mse"/"gaussian"), Poisson, negative binomial, and a "binomial" likelihood for mortality that takes a closed-cohort count pair (n_at_risk, n_died).
  • loss_weights = "auto" (the default in fit()) scales each loss by its intercept-only baseline, so the six responses are commensurable and every term reads as a fraction of its own null deviance.
  • Data helpers makeObsData(), resolveSiteIDs() and makeInitCohorts() turn a raw tree list into FINN’s input tables.
  • Model interpretation with ALE(), summary(), feature_importance() and conditionalEffects().

See the vignettes for a guided tour: Introduction to FINN, Plausible succession from a handful of species, Preparing your data for FINN, Fitting FINN to forest inventory data, and Mortality.
